checkpoints: Serializing the entire in-memory index to a single JSON blob on every mutation makes write cost proportional to the total index size rather than to the size of the change — adding one token still walks every term's posting list and every document record, so cost is O(index size) per write instead of O(delta size).

This pattern is write amplification: as the corpus grows, each small addDocument or removeDocument call pays the full-corpus serialization cost, so both CPU spent in JSON.stringify and bytes written to Redis scale with corpus size rather than with how much actually changed, causing throughput to collapse under high-ingest load even though individual writes are tiny.

The fix is to stop rewriting the whole snapshot on every mutation and instead persist only the delta — appending an operation-log entry (or a small immutable segment) per mutation — and reserve the full compacted snapshot write for a slower background schedule, so a write's cost becomes proportional to the mutation rather than to the whole index.

One incremental approach is an append-only log: push just `{ op, id, content? }` onto a Redis stream on each mutation (cheap, O(1) per write), then periodically or once the log passes a size threshold, run a full serialize-and-set to compact it; on boot, load the last full snapshot and replay the log entries after it to reconstruct an identical index.

An alternative is the Lucene segment model, where each batch of mutations becomes a new small immutable JSON segment, a background job periodically merges old segments together, and boot reads every live segment to rebuild the index.

Incremental or segment-based persistence trades away simplicity for performance: it introduces compaction/merge logic and crash-recovery bookkeeping (e.g., handling a process dying mid-append or mid-segment-write) and tombstone handling for updates/deletes, whereas the single full-snapshot write is simpler and always internally consistent — a reasonable choice for a single-node, low-ingest, or teaching-scale service.

The choice between full-snapshot and incremental persistence should be driven by ingest rate and corpus size, not treated as a correctness bug versus a solution — full-snapshot writes are a deliberate simplification whose acceptability shrinks as ingest rate and corpus size grow.

Verifying the fix requires benchmarking write latency and CPU against corpus size before (expected linear growth) and after the change (expected flat/constant cost), plus a restart or rebuild test asserting the reconstructed index is identical to the one that existed before restart.
